questions.stem: A 67 year old man has 2 months of painless visible haematuria, right loin ache and 7 kg weight loss. Today he had a focal seizure with jerking of his left arm. He has a ballotable right flank mass. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 156/90 mmHg. Haemoglobin is 186 g/L. MRI brain shows a single enhancing right frontal lesion with surrounding oedema.
questions.q: Which is the most likely primary tumour?
questions.e: Haematuria, loin pain, a flank mass and polycythaemia suggest renal cell carcinoma, a recognised source of brain metastases.

steps.x: Renal triad plus polycythaemia, then a seizure and a brain lesion.

elim: Causes haematuria but not a flank mass with polycythaemia, and rarely spreads to brain.
Gives a right upper quadrant mass, not haematuria and loin pain.
Presents with jaundice or back pain, not haematuria.
Spreads to bone, rarely to brain, and does not cause a flank mass.

steps.x: E: Renal cell carcinoma. Brain metastases come from lung, breast, melanoma, renal and colorectal cancers.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman has a 3 week history of headache and vomiting, worse in the mornings. She has noticed a hard lump in her left breast for 6 months but has not seen a doctor. She has a 3 cm irregular left breast mass with tethered skin and a hard axillary lymph node. CT head shows three lesions with surrounding oedema.
questions.q: Which is the most likely primary tumour?
questions.e: A hard, tethered breast mass with axillary nodes is breast cancer, one of the commonest sources of brain metastases.

clues: hard lump in her left breast
steps.x: Untreated breast cancer, raised ICP symptoms, multiple lesions.

elim: Rarely spreads to the brain, and nothing suggests it.
Presents with postmenopausal bleeding; rarely spreads to brain.
Spreads within the peritoneum; brain spread is rare.
No neck mass; breast findings are obvious.

steps.x: A: Breast carcinoma. Lung, breast and melanoma are the commonest sources.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman finished treatment for breast cancer 2 years ago. Her husband says that over 6 weeks she has become uncharacteristically irritable and disinhibited, and she has mild headaches. She has no past psychiatric history. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A personality change with headache in a patient with previous breast cancer suggests brain metastases (often frontal).

clues: treatment for breast cancer 2 years ago
steps.x: Previous high-risk cancer, new headache and personality change, normal calcium and sodium.

elim: Begins with memory loss, not rapid disinhibition with headache, and she is young.
Does not cause disinhibition with new headaches.
Her calcium is normal.
Her sodium is normal.

steps.x: B: Brain metastases. Suspect brain metastases in anyone with known or past cancer and new neurological symptoms.

questions.stem: A 63 year old right-handed man with lung adenocarcinoma has 2 weeks of difficulty speaking. He knows what he wants to say but speech is slow, effortful and broken. He understands commands. He has mild right arm weakness. MRI shows a 1.5 cm enhancing lesion in the left inferior frontal gyrus with surrounding oedema.
questions.q: Which is the most likely type of speech disturbance?
questions.e: A dominant inferior frontal (Broca's area) metastasis causes non-fluent expressive dysphasia with intact comprehension.

steps.x: Non-fluent speech, intact comprehension, Broca's area lesion.

elim: Slurred, scanning speech with normal language; the lesion is not cerebellar.
Poor repetition with fluent speech, from arcuate fasciculus lesions.
Comprehension is also lost; he understands commands.
Fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension, from the temporal lobe.

steps.x: C: Expressive dysphasia. Speech disturbance is a focal presentation of brain metastases; the deficit matches the site.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman with metastatic melanoma has 10 days of unsteadiness and headache. MRI shows a 2 cm enhancing lesion in the right cerebellar hemisphere with surrounding oedema. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: Cerebellar hemisphere lesions cause ipsilateral ataxia, intention tremor and dysdiadochokinesia.

steps.x: Right cerebellar metastasis.

elim: From a right occipital or optic radiation lesion, not cerebellar.
Cerebellar signs are on the same side as the lesion.
A pyramidal sign from a right hemisphere lesion.
Horner syndrome, not a cerebellar sign.

steps.x: D: Right-sided dysdiadochokinesia. Ataxia is an exam finding; cerebellar signs are ipsilateral.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with lung cancer diagnosed 4 months ago has had 3 weeks of a worsening unsteady, broad-based gait and two falls. He drinks 4 units of alcohol a week. Power and reflexes are normal. He has past-pointing and nystagmus on looking to the left.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his gait disturbance?
questions.e: New cerebellar signs in a patient with lung cancer suggest a cerebellar metastasis; gait disturbance is a classic presentation.

steps.x: Known high-risk cancer with new cerebellar signs.

elim: He drinks very little alcohol.
Causes proximal weakness with reduced reflexes, not cerebellar signs.
Causes a magnetic gait with incontinence and dementia, not nystagmus and past-pointing.
Causes a shuffling gait with rigidity, not past-pointing and nystagmus.

steps.x: B: Cerebellar metastasis. Gait disturbance and ataxia in known cancer: suspect brain metastases.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman had a bowel resection for colorectal cancer 2 years ago and now has liver metastases. She is brought in after her first seizure, which began with twitching of the left side of her face and spread to her left arm. She has no history of epilepsy or alcohol use. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her seizure?
questions.e: A new-onset seizure (here focal) in a patient with known cancer should be assumed to be an intracranial metastasis until imaging shows otherwise.

clues: twitching of the left side of her face
steps.x: Known metastatic cancer, first focal seizure, normal glucose and sodium.

elim: Her glucose is normal.
Her sodium is normal.
A new focal seizure at 64 with metastatic cancer needs a structural cause excluded.
Does not cause focal motor twitching that spreads.

steps.x: A: Brain metastasis. New seizure + known cancer = suspect brain metastasis.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer has 2 weeks of headache and mild left leg weakness. He has had no fever. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg. A CT head with contrast is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the CT head?
o: Crescentic hyperdense collection over the convexity
Hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns
Small enhancing lesion with extensive surrounding oedema
Wedge-shaped hypodensity in an arterial territory
questions.e: The classic CT appearance of a brain metastasis is a small lesion with vasogenic oedema surrounding it, often out of proportion to its size.

steps.x: Known metastatic cancer, subacute focal signs, afebrile.

elim: This is an acute subdural haematoma.
Age-related or degenerative, not a cause of new focal weakness.
This is subarachnoid haemorrhage.
This is an ischaemic infarct with sudden onset.

steps.x: D: Small enhancing lesion with extensive surrounding oedema. CT: small lesion with marked surrounding vasogenic oedema.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman with a 3 cm left cerebellar metastasis from breast cancer has 2 days of severe occipital headache and vomiting. She suddenly becomes unresponsive with irregular gasping breaths. Her pulse rate is 44 bpm and BP 194/104 mmHg. Her GCS is 5.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her deterioration?
o: Haemorrhagic stroke in the basal ganglia
Tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum
questions.e: A posterior fossa metastasis with rising ICP can push the cerebellar tonsils into the foramen magnum, compressing the brainstem: Cushing response and irregular breathing.

steps.x: Posterior fossa mass, Cushing response, failing brainstem.

elim: Follows rapid correction of hyponatraemia, not a posterior fossa mass.
Possible, but a posterior fossa mass with a Cushing response points to herniation.
Does not cause bradycardia, hypertension and irregular breathing.
Caused by a hemispheric mass, and less likely to compress the respiratory centres.

steps.x: E: Tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum. Herniation is a complication of brain metastases; posterior fossa lesions cause tonsillar herniation.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with small cell lung cancer has become increasingly confused and sleepy over a week, with morning headaches. His GCS is 13. His pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 150/88 mmHg. He takes no opioids or sedatives. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his confusion?
o: Brain metastases with raised intracranial pressure
questions.e: Small cell lung cancer often spreads to the brain; confusion, morning headache and reduced GCS with normal bloods point to brain metastases with raised ICP.

steps.x: Normal sodium, calcium and glucose: look for a structural cause.

elim: His calcium is normal.
His glucose is normal.
He takes no opioids.
Common in small cell lung cancer, but his sodium is normal.

steps.x: A: Brain metastases with raised intracranial pressure. Confusion and reduced GCS in known cancer with normal metabolic bloods = brain metastases until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman with lung cancer has 2 weeks of headaches and has twice failed to see cars coming from her right while driving. Confrontation testing shows loss of the right half of the visual field in both eyes. MRI shows a single enhancing lesion with oedema at the grey–white junction of the left occipital lobe.
questions.q: Which is the most likely visual field defect?
questions.e: A left occipital metastasis causes a contralateral (right) homonymous hemianopia; visual field defects are a classic exam finding.

clues: failed to see cars coming from her right
steps.x: Left occipital lesion; both eyes lose the right field.

elim: From optic chiasm compression, such as a pituitary tumour.
From optic nerve disease such as optic neuritis.
Would follow a right-sided lesion.
From a lesion in front of the chiasm, affecting one eye only.

steps.x: D: Right homonymous hemianopia. Occipital metastasis = contralateral homonymous hemianopia.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman with breast cancer has 2 weeks of headache and right hand clumsiness. A non-contrast CT head in the emergency department shows a single 1.5 cm left parietal lesion with surrounding oedema. The oncology team is considering focal treatment if the disease is limited. She is alert with a GCS of 15.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: CT head with contrast in 3 months
questions.e: Contrast MRI is the gold standard: it is more sensitive than CT and shows the true number of metastases, which decides between focal treatment and whole-brain treatment.

clues: focal treatment if the disease is limited
steps.x: CT shows one lesion, but CT misses small metastases.

elim: Delays diagnosis; MRI is the gold standard now.
Does not count or characterise lesions.
Unsafe with a mass lesion, and it does not image the brain.
Cannot show intracranial lesions.

steps.x: D: MRI brain with contrast. Urgent contrast MRI brain is the gold standard.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with metastatic prostate cancer and a pacemaker that is not MRI-compatible has a first generalised seizure. He is now alert. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 142/84 mmHg. Capillary glucose is 6.2 mmol/L. The team wants to look for brain metastases.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: MRI with contrast is the gold standard, but CT head is used when MRI is unavailable or unsafe, as with a non-MRI-compatible pacemaker.

steps.x: Suspected metastasis, but MRI is not possible.

elim: Does not show structural lesions.
Not the next step and unsafe if there is a mass.
The gold standard, but his pacemaker rules it out.
Not the first test for brain lesions; the brain has high background uptake.

steps.x: A: CT head with contrast. CT head if MRI is unavailable or the patient is unstable.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man with no known cancer has 3 weeks of headache. He has smoked for 40 years. MRI brain shows three enhancing lesions with surrounding oedema at the grey–white matter junction in different lobes. Physical examination, including the skin, is otherwise normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to look for the primary tumour?
questions.e: Multiple lesions at the grey–white junction suggest metastases; CT chest, abdomen and pelvis looks for the primary, most likely lung in a smoker.

steps.x: Probable metastases, primary unknown.

elim: Only if there are bowel symptoms; CT looks for the primary across the body.
Unsafe with mass lesions and does not find a primary.
Non-specific and cannot locate a primary.
Misses the lungs, the commonest source.

steps.x: B: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis. Second-line: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis to find the primary.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman has a single 2.5 cm enhancing lesion in the right frontal lobe with surrounding oedema on MRI. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis, mammography and a skin examination show no primary tumour. The team needs to know whether this is a metastasis, a primary brain tumour or an abscess before treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: When no primary is found, a biopsy gives the tissue diagnosis needed to plan treatment.

steps.x: Solitary lesion, no primary found, diagnosis uncertain.

elim: Does not give a tissue diagnosis.
Unsafe with mass effect and rarely diagnostic.
Delays diagnosis of a treatable lesion.
Non-specific and cannot give a tissue diagnosis.

steps.x: E: Stereotactic brain biopsy. Biopsy for tissue diagnosis when imaging cannot settle it.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has new headache and two enhancing brain lesions on MRI. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows a 4 cm right upper lobe lung mass with enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes. He has no tissue diagnosis. He is well enough for treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to obtain a tissue diagnosis?
o: Biopsy of the lung mass or mediastinal nodes
questions.e: CT has found the likely primary; tissue is taken from the most accessible site, here by bronchoscopic or EBUS biopsy of the lung or nodes.

clues: 4 cm right upper lobe lung mass
steps.x: Primary found on CT; tissue needed.

elim: More invasive than biopsy of the accessible chest disease.
Unsafe with mass lesions and rarely diagnostic.
Delays diagnosis and treatment.
Looks for infection, not cancer histology.

steps.x: A: Biopsy of the lung mass or mediastinal nodes. CT CAP finds the primary; biopsy the easiest site for tissue.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with brain metastases from lung cancer was started on dexamethasone 16 mg daily 3 days ago. His headache has improved. He has type 2 diabetes controlled with metformin. He is now thirsty and passing more urine.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Dexamethasone reduces oedema quickly but causes hyperglycaemia, especially in diabetes, so glucose must be monitored.

steps.x: High-dose steroids in a diabetic with osmotic symptoms.

elim: His neurological symptoms are improving.
He has no seizures.
Will be suppressed by dexamethasone and does not explain his symptoms.
Thirst with polyuria on steroids points to high glucose, not infection.

steps.x: A: Capillary blood glucose. Monitor glucose on dexamethasone.

questions.stem: A 54 year old woman with breast cancer that is well controlled outside the brain has a single 3.5 cm metastasis in the right cerebellar hemisphere. It is compressing the fourth ventricle and causing early hydrocephalus. She is independent and fully active.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
questions.e: A single, large metastasis causing mass effect in a fit patient is best removed surgically; small single lesions can have stereotactic radiosurgery.

steps.x: Single large lesion with mass effect, good performance status.

elim: She is fit with controlled disease; active treatment is appropriate.
Reduces oedema but is not definitive treatment.
Does not relieve the mass effect.
For multiple metastases; she has one large compressive lesion.

steps.x: C: Surgical resection. Single or limited metastasis: surgery or SRS; large compressive lesions favour surgery.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with lung adenocarcinoma, whose chest disease is controlled, has MRI showing three brain metastases, each under 2 cm, in different lobes. He has mild headache that has settled with dexamethasone. He works full time.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment for his brain disease?
o: Craniotomy to remove all three lesions
questions.e: A few small, discrete metastases are treated with SRS, which delivers focused high-dose radiation and spares surrounding brain.

clues: three brain metastases, each under 2 cm
steps.x: Limited small metastases in a fit patient.

elim: He is fit with controlled disease.
Three operations through separate sites carries far more risk than focused radiation.
Symptomatic only, with major side effects.
For metastases too numerous to treat focally, with more neurocognitive harm.

steps.x: D: Stereotactic radiosurgery. Limited metastases: SRS (or surgery); numerous: whole-brain RT or systemic treatment.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman with known brain metastases from melanoma is on the oncology ward. She starts having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure that has now lasted 6 minutes. She has an IV cannula. Her oxygen saturation is 93% on 15 L/min oxygen and capillary glucose is 6.8 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
questions.e: A seizure lasting over 5 minutes needs a benzodiazepine; with IV access, give IV lorazepam.

steps.x: Ongoing seizure beyond 5 minutes with IV access.

elim: Reduces oedema over hours; it does not stop a seizure.
Second-line if seizures continue after benzodiazepines.
She cannot take oral medicine while seizing.
Stop the seizure first, then image.

steps.x: C: Intravenous lorazepam. Seizures are treated appropriately: IV lorazepam first.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man with lung cancer and a known 2 cm left frontal metastasis has had worsening headache and vomiting over 24 hours. His GCS has fallen from 15 to 13. He has new right arm weakness. He is not yet on any steroids. His pulse rate is 60 bpm and BP 158/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Increase neurological observations and review tomorrow
questions.e: Worsening headache, vomiting, a new deficit and falling GCS show raised ICP: start dexamethasone and escalate urgently to neurosurgery or neuro-oncology.

steps.x: Raised ICP signs, not yet on steroids.

elim: His raised ICP needs treatment and escalation now.
Dangerous with raised ICP from a mass.
Masks worsening raised ICP.
Too slow for a falling GCS.

steps.x: A: Dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical referral. Raised ICP: dexamethasone plus urgent neurosurgical or neuro-oncology escalation.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with ovarian cancer has 10 days of headache, nausea and mild left arm weakness. MRI shows a single 1 cm right parietal lesion with a large area of surrounding oedema. Her GCS is 15. She is admitted for oncology review later in the week.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?
questions.e: Dexamethasone reduces the vasogenic oedema and mass effect, quickly relieving headache and focal symptoms.

steps.x: Symptomatic oedema around a small lesion.

elim: For acute severe ICP crisis while awaiting definitive care, not first-line here.
Only if she has seizures.
Does not treat the cause of her headache.
A chemotherapy for glioblastoma, not first-line for oedema.

steps.x: A: Dexamethasone. First-line: dexamethasone for oedema and mass effect.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with small cell lung cancer has MRI showing more than 25 metastases scattered through both cerebral hemispheres and the cerebellum. He is mobile and self-caring. His oncologist recommends brain radiotherapy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate form of radiotherapy?
o: Proton beam therapy to one lesion
questions.e: When metastases are too numerous for focal treatment, whole-brain radiotherapy treats disease throughout the brain.

clues: both cerebral hemispheres and the cerebellum
steps.x: Numerous metastases in a fit patient.

elim: Treats a single target, not widespread disease.
Not suitable when lesions are too numerous for focal treatment.
Cannot remove more than 25 lesions.
Not used for multiple brain metastases.

steps.x: E: Whole-brain radiotherapy. Multiple metastases: WBRT, SRS or systemic treatment; very many lesions favour WBRT.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with renal cell carcinoma has 2 weeks of headache. A student is told that his metastases arrived through the arterial circulation and asks where in the brain they are most likely to be seen on MRI.
questions.q: Which is the most likely location of the lesions?
questions.e: Tumour emboli travel in arteries and lodge at the grey–white junction, where vessels narrow.

steps.x: Haematogenous arterial spread.

elim: Metastases can occur here, but the commonest site is the grey–white junction.
Typical of glioblastoma (butterfly glioma) or lymphoma.
Typical of multiple sclerosis plaques or lymphoma.
Typical of pituitary adenoma.

steps.x: C: Grey–white matter junction. Metastases lodge at the grey–white junction where vessel calibre narrows.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with lung cancer has a 1 cm right frontal metastasis on MRI. T2-weighted images show finger-like bright white matter oedema spreading far beyond the lesion, sparing the overlying cortex. She has headache and left arm weakness.
questions.q: Which type of cerebral oedema is most likely?
questions.e: Tumour cells disrupt the blood–brain barrier so plasma leaks into the white matter: vasogenic oedema, often out of proportion to lesion size.

steps.x: Small lesion, extensive white matter oedema.

elim: Cell swelling from energy failure, as in early ischaemic stroke; it involves grey matter.
Caused by raised capillary pressure, as in malignant hypertension.
CSF seeps through ventricular walls in obstructive hydrocephalus.
Follows a sudden fall in plasma osmolality, such as rapid sodium correction.

steps.x: E: Vasogenic oedema. Metastases cause vasogenic oedema via blood–brain barrier disruption.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with brain metastases from melanoma has severe headache and left arm weakness. He starts dexamethasone 16 mg daily. Within 36 hours his headache has gone and his arm strength has improved, although the metastases have not changed in size on repeat imaging.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his rapid improvement?
o: Osmotic removal of water from the brain
questions.e: Dexamethasone stabilises the blood–brain barrier and reduces capillary permeability, so vasogenic oedema falls quickly and symptoms improve.

steps.x: Fast improvement without tumour shrinkage.

elim: The lesions have not shrunk; steroids do not kill metastases.
Would raise ICP, not lower it.
This is how mannitol works.
He has not had seizures; steroids are not antiepileptic.

steps.x: D: Reduced blood–brain barrier capillary permeability. Dexamethasone works by stabilising the blood–brain barrier.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman with breast cancer has two brain metastases, each 1.5 cm, in the right frontal and left parietal lobes. She is treated with stereotactic radiosurgery. A medical student asks why this was chosen.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate explanation?
o: It gives focused high-dose radiation that spares surrounding brain
It is the only option that treats microscopic disease throughout the brain
It needs a craniotomy to reach the lesions
It works by shrinking the oedema rather than the tumour
questions.e: SRS focuses high-dose radiation onto small targets while sparing nearby tissue, so it suits a few discrete metastases.

steps.x: Few, small, discrete metastases.

elim: SRS is a form of radiation.
That describes whole-brain radiotherapy.
SRS is non-invasive; no craniotomy is needed.
That is how dexamethasone helps.

steps.x: B: It gives focused high-dose radiation that spares surrounding brain. SRS: focused, high-dose, tissue-sparing, for limited disease.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with lung cancer has more than 20 brain metastases and is offered whole-brain radiotherapy rather than stereotactic radiosurgery. His wife asks what the main long-term downside of whole-brain treatment is.
questions.q: Which is the most likely long-term adverse effect?
questions.e: Whole-brain radiotherapy treats disease throughout the brain but causes greater neurocognitive side effects, such as memory problems, than focused SRS.

steps.x: Whole-brain treatment for numerous lesions.

elim: Brain radiotherapy does not irradiate significant bone marrow.
Follows neck irradiation, not whole-brain radiotherapy.
Follows chest radiotherapy.
Follows pelvic radiotherapy.

steps.x: C: Neurocognitive decline. WBRT cost: neurocognitive decline.
